html:
This section talks about the role offline (non-interactive) learning in human learning, especially relative to online (interactive) learning

The "Offline Learning" section should be pruned and sharpened. It currently reads as a comprehensive review of sleep and replay literature. For the Principles section, what matters is: what does offline learning accomplish that online learning cannot, and why? The answer is: (1) prioritized replay for sample efficiency, (2) model-based imagination for counterfactual training, (3) representational reorganization for interference reduction, (4) synaptic homeostasis as complexity regularization. Make those four points crisply and defer the detailed neurophysiology to the Systems Architecture section.

Credit assignment via offline branching sim

"Planning" in the broadest sense; it is meant to convey that offline learning is squarely future-oriented

There is constantly a queue of memories to be processed, which are augmented many times over artificially/synthetically. Does this explain human "generalization"?

New structure

Compression/abstraction

Consolidation/reorganization

Synthetic data generation and planning

Counterfactual simulation is critical for generating new knowledge

Carvalho’s work 1

Data pipeline: observe, explore, and narrate; sleep; repeat

Offline learning is both retrospective and prospective

We often spend time escaping the present by remembering events from the past (episodic memory), imagining how those past events might have turned out differently (episodic counterfactual thinking), thinking about how the future will unfold (episodic future thinking), or daydreaming about events that we know will never transpire (fictional thinking) 2

Sufficient conditions for offline reactivation in recurrent neural networks

Frame offline learning as the other half of the optimizer. Give a mechanistic pass first: during NREM, hippocampal ripples coordinated by slow-oscillation->spindle nesting replay tagged episodes; dopaminergic salience biases which traces are selected; REM then delivers dendritic plateaus that prune and stabilize structural changes. Tie this to three algorithmic payoffs. First, sample efficiency via prioritized replay that focuses updates on states with high temporal-difference error or high epistemic value. Second, model-based imagination: generative world models (hippocampus-DMN) produce synthetic rollouts that let the actor/critic learn from counterfactuals it never executed. Third, representational reorganization: replay "remixes" features so that neocortical codes become sparser and more linearly separable, reducing interference. Make it pragmatic for AGI/robotics: separate an online learner (fast, low-variance, small steps, strict safety budget) from an offline learner (large-batch, distributional-RL critics, conservative policy updates from logged data, heavy model-based imagination), and add a targeting mechanism analogous to targeted memory reactivation to steer which skills/episodes are consolidated after each deployment day.

Since the seminal work of Marr in 1971 [], the notion that offline replay plays a key role in learning has received a wealth of supporting evidence. Progress has been made in identifying the key characteristics and functions of replay in the context of the three "offline" behavioral states: NREM sleep, also called "slow wave" and "deep" sleep; REM sleep; and wakeful rest. Each of these states contributes uniquely to behavior, facilitating the construction and transformation of generalized representations in the brain []. In this section, the characteristics and functions of replay are mostly described in the context of each offline behavioral state independently, then are synthesized into key takeaways.

History of systems consolidation theories

Standard model of systems consolidation posits that episodic memories are converted into semantic memories, implying they are transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex. Under this model, it has been assumed that remote episodic memories reflect semanticized versions of the original memories (personal semantics) that are independent of the hippocampus.

Multiple trace theory (MTT) posited that episodic memories, no matter how remote, always depend on the hippocampus, while semantic memories are supported by cortical modules.

Trace Transformation Theory (TTT) took these ideas a step further and proposed that memories’ substrates are adaptively determined according to task demands, emphasizing that semantic and episodic memories continually communicate, can coexist, and cooperate at retrieval-time. This model emphasizes the concept of "neural-psychological correspondence", which states that neural transformations directly reflect psychological transformations (e.g transforming a perceptually detailed episodic memory into a "gist-like" episodic memory means going from posterior HPC to anterior HPC and mPFC)

Credit assignment, counterfactual planning

Unified view: replay according to expected utility of computing trajectories

Mattar and Daw 2018 produce a model that accounts for forward and reverse replay

Condition replay on expected utility of visiting each state; reverse replay for propagating new information to previous locations and forward replay for prospection based on past trajectories

Sequential neural activity in humans has similarly been observed to exhibit orderings consistent with sampling based on future need. Using a statistical learning task with graphlike dependencies between visual cues (Schapiro et al., 2013; Garvert et al., 2017; Lynn et al., 2020), Wittkuhn et al. (2022) showed participants a series of animal images drawn from a ring-like graph structure in either a uni- or bi-directional manner. Using fMRI data recorded during 10s pauses between trials, Wittkuhn et al. (2022) found forward and reverse sequential activity patterns in visual and sensorimotor cortices, a pattern well-captured by an SR model learnt from the graph structure participants experienced.

Goal-conditioned traversal of past, present, and future environments according to information gain

More on this in NREM section

Replay During NREM Sleep

Qualities of NREM sleep

brain-wide synchronization []

hippocampal excitability []

cortical plasticity []

regularly occurring sharp wave ripple (SWR) events, which are bursts of activity in the hippocampus that have been shown to implement replay on a compressed timescale []

Sharp wave ripples often coincide with "sleep spindles", which are bursts of thalamo-cortical activity that further coincide with the "up" states of slow waves; slow waves provide a global temporal framework for the coordination of nested oscillatory programs []

SWRs and sleep spindles have repeatedly and reliably been causally linked to memory performance across all memory types [], with their disruption during NREM sleep often leading to the complete prevention of learning []

History of replay during NREM sleep

first observed during NREM sleep in the 1994 work of Wilson and McNaughton [], where the authors demonstrated that populations of hippocampal cells which fired together during a spatial navigation task were more likely to fire together during subsequent NREM sleep

In 1996, it was then shown that these cells were reactivated in an order matching the original, waking experience []

These findings provided evidence for longstanding theories of systems consolidation, which posited that newly acquired information is transferred from short-term (hippocampal) to long-term (cortical) storage during sleep [] (Figure [fig:transfer]).

Today, it is widely held that NREM sleep represents the most focused and vigorous period of replay [], which is known to be goal-directed (see "Selective Replay"), abstractive (see "Generalization and Abstraction"), and generative []

Recent work also scrutinizes the notion of memories being "transferred" from short-term memory to long-term memory during NREM replay, instead opting for a model which posits that memories’ neural substrates are proactively determined in response to and in anticipation of task demands (see "Beyond ...")

Modern functional view of NREM replay

All fall under the umbrella of preparing for the future by processing the past; basic need to prevent ill-preparedness at inference-time 13; also results in less compute overall if you trade sleep-time compute for inference-time compute

Basic need for repetition for robust integration 14; synaptic consolidation

Interleaved learning

Not bound by ongoing experience

Humans and neural network models learn faster (especially in terms of conceptual relatedness) when diverse concepts are interleaved instead of blocked 15, 16, 17

Supports all kinds of representations

Structural abstraction, in the general case

Extraction of "gist" representations of experiences []

Packaging/compressing them for retrieval and generalization

Semantic memories

Integrating distant experiences into new knowledge

Schematic memories

Schemas are superordinate knowledge structures that reflect abstracted commonalities across several experiences []. A cognitive structure must satisfy the following criteria to be considered a schema: abstraction over several experiences; associative structure; lack of unit detail; and adaptability []. One example of a schema is a network of neural representations encoding the usual behaviors and events of a typical birthday party (an event schema) [], and another is the usual layout of a modern city (a spatial schema) [].

The associative, abstract, and adaptive nature of schemas make them uniquely positioned to benefit from the offline, replay-based learning

Offline replay allows brains to perform focused reasoning over new experiences in tandem with any of the cognitive structures and experiences held in the vast repositories supported by biological brains (Figure [fig:transfer])

Biomarkers for the abstraction and integration of experiences include reduced hippocampal activation during a task [] and increased functional connectivity among distributed memory traces

Schemas gradually develop with repeated exposure and consolidation []

NREM assimilates new info into existing schemas 18

Maps of specific events and environments 19; reduced similarity between hippocampal representations measured during task exposure and across NREM sleep 20

Model-free policies 21 and task representations 22; forging a generalizable representation of the world can be seen as creating a model-free policy or as caching results for reuse

Selective and generative

Most informative experiences are simulated, including synthetic experiences; can be seen as planning 21

"rank order correlation between neuronal firing sequences during slow-wave sleep or awake rest and future novel place-cell sequences on a previously unexplored linear context" 23

Waking offline replay as dynamic consolidation

Selectivity

Perhaps the most well-studied and predictable aspect of selective replay is its preference for experiences including large rewards

Large reward prediction errors 21

Recency (which accounts for the observed "transfer" of memories from the hippocampus to the cortex) []; however, a large fraction of offline replay’s contents appear to not be recency-biased 24; remote replay is especially clear in dreaming 25

Number of times an experience/task was repeated or was apart of waking replay

NREM replay has also been shown to be less sequential and more fragmented/partial than waking replay

Potential balancing effect via replay?: "Another study of goal oriented navigation showed that while animals spent the most time physically in the proximity of a reward location in real time, replay reduces this behavioral bias by upsampling regions of space in which less time was spent (Grosmark et al. 2021)"

Initial replay builds a rough draft, later replays fill in the gaps: Berners-Lee et al. (2022) found that replays appear after single exposures and slow down while increasing in resolution with repeated experience

One intriguing proposition is that, during offline replay, the hippocampus implements a sort of similarity-weighted retrieval over abstract cortical representations []. Such selectivity could minimize the degree to which new representations interfere with overlapping representations, along with maximizing learning speed []. On top of the computational evidence presented in the original work [], recent work has bolstered the original claim with more sophisticated modeling techniques []

Replay should support generalization of world models and therefore should focus on "predictable" episodes; may be actualized in brains and has seen success in ML

Can show this computationally 26

Predictable stimuli vs random are replayed in mice 27

Maybe the appearance of selective replay being geared towards emotional experiences is correlational; replay should focus on revealing environmental dynamics

Although the extent to which similar, remote, and "predictable" memories are retrieved during offline replay remain open questions, existing demonstrations of selective replay tease out another one of the main benefits of offline, replay-based learning: the high degree of cortical plasticity afforded during offline learning is utilized by the most relevant and information-dense experiences, as a purely online learning algorithm would need to constantly update synaptic connections since the learner would always be unsure of whether previous or future experiences will carry the most (or any) information regarding the world’s latent structure []; without carefully optimizing the "training data" fed into the cortex, overfitting and inefficiency take hold []. As the saying goes, hindsight is 20/20.

While the hippocampus likely contributes to these simulations, classifying them as "replay" seems misguided since they are far from recapitulations of waking experiences, altough substantial evidence implies that the contents of dreams are strongly biased towards recent events (Daytime exp..)

Most studies have been focused on either wake or sleep

Greater "sequenceness" and locality [] than NREM

Lack of sequenceness in sleep may reflect active transformation of memories or the simultaneous activation of multiple memories undergoing integration

May also reflect greater selectivity

Waking replay: local, exploratory, initiation, and substantial work + actual novel planning which overlaps in nature and function with online replay -> NREM replay: continued consolidation + nonlocal + system integration

Substrate of rapid memory integration?

Waking SWRs tag experience for offline replay; related to repetition bias (Wannan Yang, Selection of exp...)

What is the training data / training pipeline of the DMN?: Complementary learning systems and online/offline learning regimes

The learning problem, stated cleanly: the DMN is not trained on a continuous sensory stream. It is trained on a curated, temporally restructured, value-tagged set of internal "replays" and "simulations" whose job is to turn (i) a long tail of idiosyncratic episodes into (ii) a small set of predictive latent variables (schemas, narratives, social models, self-model) that generalize. This is why "rest" and sleep are not idling–they are the brain’s dataset construction + optimization loop for high-level generative structure 30.

Architectural precondition: the DMN is already a memory-simulation composite (core + medial temporal + dorsal-medial subsystems), i.e., it is physically interleaved with the very machinery that provides its training samples (hippocampus/MTL) and the machinery that stores abstractions (mPFC/PCC/AG). 31.

Complementary learning systems

The brain’s architecture reflects a split between "raw data buffering" and "compressed model storage," codified in the Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) framework. The hippocampus acts as a fast-learning buffer for episodic details (high fidelity, low compression), while the neocortex (specifically the DMN apex) acts as a slow-learning repository for statistical regularities (lossy, high compression). Systems consolidation is the off-line optimization process where the brain distills the chaotic log of daily experience into the structured, low-dimensional manifold of the cortical model 32, 33.

The human brain utilizes a dual-store architecture to manage the accuracy/complexity trade-off over time:

The Fast/High-Complexity Store (Hippocampus): Rapidly encodes episodic experiences with high fidelity via pattern separation. This minimizes immediate prediction error but carries a high "description length" or complexity cost.

The Slow/Compressed Store (Neocortex/DMN): Over time, these high-dimensional episodes are "replayed" and interleaved with existing knowledge to extract invariants. By the time information reaches the DMN, it has been stripped of idiosyncratic noise and integrated into schemas 34, 35.

The DMN’s learning is not a single mechanism–it is an alternation between online data acquisition and offline dataset distillation, i.e., a true online/offline regime split.

Training data: what actually "feeds" the DMN?

Indexed episodes (high-fidelity tokens) from hippocampus: sparse bindings of "what/where/when" plus relational structure; these are the seed points for later semanticization. 36, 37.

Event-structured transitions (state sequences rather than static snapshots): what matters for compression is predictive structure–how latent states evolve. Replay often appears sequential, as if the brain is rehearsing trajectories through a learned state graph. 38, 39.

Schema priors and "explanation frames" from mPFC/DMN core: existing concepts, scripts, and social models that new episodes must either be assimilated into or force accommodation (schema update / creation). This makes learning conditional: the same episode trains different hypotheses depending on the current schema. 40, 41.

Value/affect tags attached to episodes (salience-weighting): reward, threat, curiosity/uncertainty, goal relevance–these act like sample weights that change replay probability and plasticity gain. 42, 43.

Self-generated "synthetic data": counterfactuals, future events, social rehearsals, narrative recombinations. These samples are not veridical, but they are structurally consistent with learned priors and therefore useful for training a generative model (data augmentation / regularization). 44, 45.

The DMN’s learning is not a single mechanism–it is an alternation between online data acquisition and offline dataset distillation, i.e., a true online/offline regime split.

Stage 1 – Online (wake): acquisition + tagging (construct the replay buffer)

Encode: hippocampus rapidly indexes episodes; cortex/DMN extracts coarse gist online (enough to guide behavior), but defers heavy compression. 37.

Tag: neuromodulators assign priority labels (reward, novelty, uncertainty, threat, goal relevance), determining what will be replayed and with what plasticity gain. Think of this as "importance sampling" for the offline learner. 46, 43.

Early integration when schemas exist: mPFC can bias encoding/retrieval toward schema-consistent features (rapid assimilation) or highlight prediction-violating features (schema update). This is a key inductive bias: the DMN is trained to prefer explanations that reuse existing latent factors when possible. 40, 41.

Stage 2 – Offline (quiet wake / rest): replay-driven "mini-batch updates"

Offline learning is not only sleep. During awake rest, hippocampus expresses replay and the cortex expresses reinstatement; importantly, there is direct evidence that hippocampal sharp-wave ripples are followed by increased DMN (BOLD) activity, consistent with ripples acting like "commit events" that write episodic minibatches into DMN-level representations. 47, 48.

Replay during rest is selective: it often prioritizes weaker or high-utility memories (not simply the most recent), consistent with a learning system that is actively reducing uncertainty / improving generalization. 39.

Computationally, this is where the DMN can run controlled internal rollouts: hippocampus provides the state sequence; DMN provides the generative "world model" and tries to compress it into reusable latent causes; control networks can gate which rollouts are pursued.

Stage 3 – Offline (NREM sleep): high-bandwidth transfer + schema writing

NREM is the canonical regime for active systems consolidation: hippocampal replay events (sharp-wave ripples) are temporally coordinated with cortical slow oscillations and thalamocortical spindles, creating windows where hippocampal patterns can effectively train cortical networks. 49, 50, 51.

This tri-oscillation choreography is a structure-preserving bottleneck–it compresses time (replay is time-compressed), sparsifies updates (discrete ripple events), and interleaves new episodes with old knowledge (spindle/slow-oscillation mediated cortical context), which is exactly what you want for extracting invariants without overwriting.

The DMN’s role here is plausibly: (i) integrate across modalities (transmodal hub property), (ii) map episodes onto schemas (mPFC), and (iii) update narrative/social/self latents that require long temporal integration. Recent work explicitly discusses DMN-hippocampus involvement in consolidation across sleep/wake regimes. 52.

Stage 4 – Offline (REM sleep): generative recombination + affective reweighting

REM shifts the optimization profile: rather than faithful replay, REM is well-positioned for hyperassociative recombination (dream-like simulation), abstraction, and emotional retagging–useful for training a generative model to capture broader structure and for updating value priors. 53, 54.

The neuromodulatory milieu differs sharply across stages (e.g., acetylcholine/norepinephrine/serotonin dynamics), changing both what gets replayed and how plasticity is expressed, i.e., the brain effectively changes its optimizer settings across sleep stages. 46, 55.

Global regularization: synaptic homeostasis as "compression pressure"

In parallel to targeted replay-based updates, sleep may implement a cortex-wide normalization/downscaling that acts like a complexity penalty (prevent runaway growth of synaptic strength; improve SNR; keep representational capacity usable). This pairs naturally with the "drive for compression" framing: replay writes useful structure; downscaling removes diffuse, low-utility potentiation. 56, 57.
